newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-Australian stocks, bonds to surge.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-Australian stocks, bonds to surge.

text.p: Australian bond and stock markets are expected to start the week strongly after Wall Street and U.S. treasuries rallied sharply on Friday night on softer than expected inflation data and the subsequent easing of Fed rate hike fears.

But the Australian dollar is likely to open with a weaker bias after falling to US$0.7905 in New York trade from its US$79.65 local close on Friday as the CRB index fell in line with oil prices and easing tensions in the Persian gulf. A fall through support at US$0.7950 was seen as bearish. However it has bounced slightly in early New Zealand trade.
U.S. bonds and stocks roared ahead on Friday night after the consumer price index, closely watched by the Fed and Wall Street, rose 0.1 percent for August, below the expected 0.2 percent.
August retail sales rose 0.2 percent, well below the anticipated 0.7 percent.

"Goldilocks is back -- the (U.S.) economy is not too hot or too cold," said David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers. "This is the kind of environment where we'll have a Dow 6000 by the election."
The Dow industrials jumped 67 to an unofficial record of 5839. The long bond soared 1-17/32 to yield 6.95 percent.
Looking ahead through the week, there is little domestic economic data and few corporate results seen likely to shunt the markets around.
"Developments in the U.S. Treasury market should therefore continue to be the main driving force," said Bain and Co's economists in their weekly preview.
One of the most significant events of this week will be the changing of the Reserve Bank Governor.
Bernie Fraser, retires on Tuesday after seven years in the job replaced by one of his current Deputies, Ian Macfarlane, an appointment which was announced last month.

The data calander is filled mainly with partial indicators that do not generally capture the markets' attention, although there are a couple of business surveys released that could impact on market sentiment.

The major data of the week is Wednesday's merchandise imports for August. A 2.2 percent rise is the median forecast, reflecting the view that while import demand remians soft, after three months of weakness, a softer Australian dollar and the
likely inclusion of a A$100 million plane, a rise is likely.

Of the minor data, consumer sentiment also on Wednesday will also be important in assessing just how the public reacted to the budget last month, and also the jump in the August unemployment rate to 8.8 percent.

The State Bank of New South Wales and the Australian Business Chamber survey of NSW manufacturing will be out first thing on Monday, and Westpac and the Australian Chamnber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) business survey will be release don Wednesday.
These surveys will update business intentions in areas such as sales, prices, employment, and quite importantly, investment.
Given the budget's strong 14 percent forecast growth in business investment, signs of weakness here could lead to building rate cut expectations.

The Reserve Bank Bulletin will be released on Monday. The article will contain the introductory chapter of the RBA's 1996 confernece volume "The Future of the Financial System," which will be released at the same time.
BONDS (Friday: 10 year bonds 8.10, 3 year 7.20)

The Australian bond market should start the week with a strong tone after U.S. Treasuries rallied sharply on Friday's CPI report, which cast serious doubt on the once-certain prospect of an imminent Fed rate hike.
Conversely, the local market is again starting to build in the possibility of a further cut in official interest rates by the Reserve Bank before year-end.
The unexpected 8.8 percent rise in the unemployment rate in August, reported last Thursday, has rekindled hopes of an easing from the current level of 7.0 percent.

"For the past six months, jobs growth has been anaemic, job ads are drying up, building approvals remain down in the dumps and retail sales growth has slowed," said economists at State Bank New South Wales in their weekly report.
"Add to this the cuts made in the budget and a case exists for lower interest rates," they added.

Meanwhile, the bond futures market could see a flurry activity in the first half of today's trade as as the last stages of the rollover into December contracts go through ahead of the midday close-outs of September three- and 10-year positions.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri: 0.7962/67, New York US$0.7902/09)
The Australian dollar ended local trading on a softer note and fell on Friday, after offshore sentiment favouring a rate cut grew on the release of the higher unemployment rate.
It is seen opening weak as well after a drop through key supports in New York on Friday night.
The key event for the markets early in the week is not an data, but the rumoured expiry of an option strangle placed by an Asian player well prepared to support the position.

Traders said on Friday the strangle was set at US$0.7950/8050, and was seen expiring late on Monday, although some doubted its existence. The parameters are important because US$0.7950 is seen as an important support level, and a breach could see the AUD back under US$0.7900.
Market sentiment in the lead up to the U.S. FOMC on September 24 will also play on the AUD.
The easing of U.S. rate hike fears may help the Australian dollar, keeping a wide prospective gap in short interest rate differentials between the United States and Australia.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ordinaries 2252.3, up 15.7)

Wall Street's run into record high territory on Friday is seen as the early driver in the Australian stock market this week, although the general tone was already seen as upbeat after a recovery in the major miners late last week.
"I think it is likely to go higher. The miners may still have some left in them," said a Sydney broker, pointing to share prices that have largely factored in weaker metals prices.
The broker also noted that with the results season reaching a conclusion, investors may well go looking for bargains after analysing the figures.
"Results are out of the road and now people have looked at them more closely, we may see some selective buying," he said.
Corporate news-wise, while June 30 results are complete, other companies continue to report and retailers David Jones and Country Road check in next week.
David Jones is first off the rank on Tuesday while Country Road is due on Friday, which also sees first quarter results from Friday's late charger, bellwether BHP.
Economic data due next week is relatively minor and unlikely to cause much concern in equities market.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
